paragraphs.text: Whether in a large city or a small town, the opera season was the centre of social life in 18th-century Italy – for the nobility, their servants, and such middle-class people as an impoverished country could show: lawyers, doctors, army officers, a few bankers, and merchants and even a good many priests and monks. Only the grandest theatres specialised exclusively in opera, the very grandest, the San Carlo in Naples and La Fenice in Venice (opened in 1732), staged nothing but opera seria, the style based on historical events or mythology, whose themes had been regarded through most of the 18th century as appropriate entertainment for kings. The operas were frequently accompanied by virtuosic singing and brilliant top support the singing. Most other theatres put on a variety of performances, not only opera (serious or comic) but plays, occasional concerts by visiting instrumentalists, equestrian or acrobatic displays, and even performing monkeys.

The theatre calendar was carefully arranged. Opera, as everyone knew, was the most exalted genre and, within opera, opera seria was its supreme form. A particular season, usually Carnival (running from 26 December until early spring), was the most fashionable one in which to show opera seria. Lesser genres, such as comic opera, were put on in other seasons or, if the city had more than one theatre, in less fashionable venues. These distinctions were marked in the most practical ways: in fashionable seasons or theatres it cost more to get in and the audiences were correspondingly more aristocratic. Nor was admission to opera left in the free play of market forces: it was laid down in detail by government regulation. A season commonly offered two operas, with were as a rule two new and often newly commissioned. Each might be performed twenty times, unless it was a total disaster, in which case a third, ‘fall-back’ opera might have to be put on in a hurry to take its place.

In the 18th-century Italy's for the upper classes, as foreign visitors often remarked, did not entertain much in their freezing houses; they were virtually impossible to heat or light to any degree of magnificence, and so they were often shut off from it. It was indeed the height of the theatre season that the country was at its most pleasurable and was the season. Not only did one talk to friends in the noisy intervals between operas, but among performers too, bondage musicians developed strong hostages attached to the friends they played good and drunk. In addition, the theatres had large handsome foyers – the main purpose of which was to accommodate the playing of games such as roulette or backgammon. An Italian could thus spend a large part of his year making life in a high style without discomfort for relatively little money. The French novelist Stendhal wrote from Milan in 1814, 'A good citizen of Milan has a fine time from a quarter past seven until half past midnight, taking in marvellous things.'

In these conditions, it is not surprising that Italian audiences were regarded by foreign visitors as the noisiest in Europe – this at a time when no audience anywhere kept totally silent. People might be relatively quiet during the ballet, the German composer Otto Nicolai reported, ‘but during the opera they all chatter like canary birds that cry all the more sharply the louder the music is played.’ There is some exaggeration here: even at the twentieth performance, people paid attention to an aria or a duet they admired. When they listened, they did so phrase by phrase, and they might whistle the Italian equivalent of hissing with disapproval at a note sung flat the moment after they had cheered a beautifully-performed melody. The Italian audience was not unlike the crowd at some modern sporting events; noise was fairly common. They wanted displays of skill, not just from singers but from composers and scene designers as well. Within a narrow range of experience, people were highly knowledgeable and eager for new enjoyments, but they were conservative and would tolerate only small changes, whether in the form of the music or in styles of singing or playing.

Even with so conservative an audience, Italian music changed, but it did so gradually over a long period. Alongside opera seria, audiences started to enjoy comic opera which had its golden age in the late 18th century. The great successes of the period were nearly all comic operas, most of them now forgotten. Their subjects, because of the censorship exercised by all the Italian states, were full of harmless clichés. The bad-tempered old man fooled by his clever maid, the vanity of rival opera singers, the comic foreigner and so on. The music too can sound to us remarkably similar from one work to the next. Because rapid action was essential to the success of comic opera, singers' vocal lines could be less elaborate and demanding than was the norm in opera seria. Good acting was not ignored in opera seria, but in comic works, it counted for a good deal more than how well the performer could sing.
